newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan pledge clears way for nuclear storage plan.
newsitem.headline: Japan pledge clears way for nuclear storage plan.

text.p: Japan's commitment to its ambitious nuclear energy programme is expected to help clear the way for the opening of a much-needed nuclear fuel storage facility, officials and industry sources said on Wednesday.
The Atomic Energy Commission, the ultimate arbiter of Japan's nuclear policy, said last week that Japan has no plans to alter its nuclear policy even after recurring accidents at nuclear facilities.

Morio Kimura, governor of Aomori prefecture, where the new storage facility is located, welcomed the sign that Japan was standing behind its nuclear agenda, according to a Science and Technology Agency official.

The official, along with other officials from the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI), visited Aomori in northern Japan over the weekend to explain personally to the governor the commission's statement.

The storage facility in Aomori was originally scheduled to receive small amounts of spent fuel in June for testing purposes, and to start accepting used fuel from nuclear power plants across the country in October.

However, a fire and explosion accident at Japan's Tokaimura nuclear fuel reprocessing plant in March, which exposed 37 workers to low-level radiation, derailed talks on safety measures for the new storage facility.
As a result, the start-up date for the storage facility has been postponed indefinitely, raising questions as to what Japan will do with its rising stockpiles of spent nuclear fuel.
Kimura, in order to assuage growing local concern over the facility's fate, had called on the government to clarify its latest stance on Japan's nuclear programme.
Japan Nuclear Fuel Ltd, operator of the Aomori storage facility, gave a guarded welcome to the government's reassurances.

"We may call it (the issuance of the statement) one step forward to the start-up of the storage facility, in a sense that it helped lessen local residents' anxiety over the future of Japan's nuclear programme," a company spokesman said.

However, the operator has not heard from local authorities on when talks will resume on the plant's safety measures, which are necessary for the storage facility to start accepting spent nuclear fuel.

Some temporary storage facilities for spent fuel at nuclear power plants are expected to run out of capacity at around 2000 to 2002 unless fuel can be shipped out to the Aomori storage facility or additional storage is constructed on-site.
The storage facility in Aomori is a part of a new 800-tonne-a-year nuclear fuel reprocessing plant, slated to start commercial operations in 2003.
